blocks.x: We're going if you want to put your name on here, you can start off so we don't have no identify the tape and you can just talk naturally, you don't pick up anything in the
room. Yeah, I want to ask any questions, don't I?

We want to get your name first. What is your name? Andrew Andy, Joe Anderson. Why is it Joe? Musician gave me the name. Do you have any other middle name though? Can you tell us just where you were born?
I was born in a little town called Manneville, Louisiana.
Across the lake?
Across the lake, yeah. Bunk used to come over there on the weekends to play. You remember? Yeah, he played with my daddy, he used to play bass over there.
When were you born? What was your birthday?
I hate to tell everybody my birthday, but nevertheless since it's... This is part of history. It's history. None of your friends will hear this. I was born August 10th, 1905.
About the same age as me then, a little bit younger than me.

Well I was born August 10th, 1905 and all around the house there, you know I always had inspiration to play music. My daddy tried to get me to play drums. You know I always talked to him about a set of drums. Because they needed a drummer in their band, you see they had, they called that band a spasm band. They had three-piece. They had a violin, guitar, and string bass. And so one day my brother saw a cornet, one of the short brass cornet. He bought the cornet for twelve dollars. So he came around the house, he never could play anything on them. So my daddy was still trying to get me to play drums, see. I said I picked up the trumpet, this cornet one day, an old man, they call him Manny Gabriel, he's an old musician, you know. He's a trumpet player. And the boat used to come over the lake there, it started a camellia. He made a red of it, on the river there, a camellia. Well they used to come over on Sundays and there's a tune I loved to hear him play. And that was, what's the name of the tune again? I can't think of. Pomet. Thailand stuff you know, but everyone knew what I was trying to play. So there's another fellow called Black Eagle, he and I started out together, so first little job we played some people, white people hired us to play for a party. We two went back then to play for the party, first little job we played. And I came on back and he never did decide to read Miss or to read Miss, so I came on back and I got out of that one and learned how to read Miss. So the first lesson I took was Mr. Parrish, he's an old Mortimer, I call his white fellow, he looks the scales out, the scales out for me. The first lesson I took was from him. So I decided when I came to New Orleans in 1919, I was in the American School of Music, you know, home and coast, so I decided to send him off for this home and coast. So I sent off for it, that was in around 1922 I think that it was, before that, but anyway during the time I was in front. So when I sent for this course I had took about, I guess about 14, 12, 14 lessons. And Willie Forster, Pop Forster's brother, you know, Pop Forster's brother, heard about me up there, he was up living uptown playing trumpet. So he came to my house and asked me about playing, see. So I told him, I said, well I'm not good enough to play yet, I said, but I'm going to go take a few lessons, I went to pitch back. Tiro, he was the head of the PWA band, you know, the head and you know. So after I went by him to take lessons, he asked me, say, boy who's been teaching you? I said, no one. I said, I've been taking correspondence. He said, well I'll be doggone, people tell me you can't learn that way. He said, well you better know some scholars I've been teaching two years. I said, you can read better some scholars I've been teaching two years. Well I inspired you, I gave you inspiration to go on, you know. So I came back and told Willie Forster, yes I can play in your band. So he got his band, I tell you, me playing trumpet, Bigger Ennis Keller, Leda Ennis Keller. He had Albert Fader, I don't know if he's living still, but Crump, Lil Crump, Leda Trump, he's playing saxophone. We had the Sun Johnson, you all know him, I know. I've never heard of him, I know, Sun Johnson, his name is Augustine Johnson, we all call him Sun. A lot of the fellas call him Bobo, you know. So we got him, the four of us, Willie Forster, and his son-in-law rather, and we started playing out there, bunk up to the space, every Friday, Saturday night, that's below the, on the other side of the levee, you know. We played out there. And through playing with him, Frank Jarrett heard about me on the Pelican. He needed a trumpet player. So he came up, called him and got, and I said, man we need a trumpet player. So I went on the Pelican, started playing with the Pelican. Well that's where the name, the Pelican Silverstone was, and I still use it, you know. I use it, the Black Pelicans, that's where I use it now. We started on the Pelican. Well I played on the Pelican about, let's see, now I'm sure, it must have been about three years. About three years, yeah. Well after we got the band there on the Pelican, the band was so good in reading music and playing music, until Miss Amber Lily Mae Hubbard, she used to come in singing the band and kind of coach the band, you know. She was a member of the Green Pastures. She was singing in Green Pastures. Now she used to go to New York and buy anything. She'd buy overtures for us to play with a ten piece band, see. She just thought we could play anything. I'll tell you, one number she bought for us, Headlow, that's one of the numbers she bought for us, and it brought another one, Listernia, that was another one. We played that. We also played Louisiana Bobo, we were the first band down there to play Louisiana Bobo. So the band got good and you know how the older fellas are, when they see young men coming up and they're good, they come pick out just who they want out of the band, see. The main others, they just try to tear the band down and keep them doing them some more, you know. I found out later, you know, later, but I didn't know the other thing. So first man that come and got out of the band, Alvin Alcorn was playing second trumpet with me, man. Alvin Alcorn, they took Alvin Alcorn out of the band, Don Amber did that, took Alvin Alcorn out of the band. No, it wasn't, no it wasn't, Alvin Alcorn, had a professor, he taught at school at, Professor Dedeson, he taught at school at New Orleans University at that time, New Orleans I think it's Dillard now. He took Alvin Alcorn, Frank Jackhead, which was the leader of the band, you know, he was the leader of the trombone player there. And he took Jim, the bass tuba player, the human bass tuba there. He took our bass tuba player, I can't think of his name, it was the name of the band, and how he took the three men out. Well that led me to have to get, replace three men, see. I replaced Alvin Alcorn with Leo Dejong. And I replaced Frank with, what's this old man, Sonny Henry, Sonny Henry. Sonny Henry and I replaced the bass play with Boise Gregg, his name, you know. He was an old show man. He was a great trumpet player also, you know, played bass too. But he replaced them. Well about time the band got pretty good, well they took some other men out of the band, see them? They took Sonny Johnson out of the band. Sonny Johnson, that's who else they took. I remember Sonny, the one, he was playing first sax. And, oh yeah, the piano player had left that time, so we got Emily Hyman was playing with, late Emily Hyman, she was playing with us during that time. We got Camilla Todd, you know Camilla Todd is Clarence Todd's brother, our sister brother, you know. And Clarence Todd. You remember Clarence Todd from, he's in Chicago, he's a piano player, he's arranging, we call him steeplehead, he's got a head like a steeplehead.
Somebody made, there was Clarence Williams.
Clarence Todd, they got Clarence Williams and they got Clarence Todd.
Clarence Todd had made some records of Clarence Williams, that's what I'm trying to think of, a singer too, did he sing?

Clarence Todd, he did. That's the same song. We can talk to Camilla sometime. Yeah, he was, not so very long ago he was there, you know. Camilla lives uptown. And I also, for Alvin, I got Lois Domain, you know, Lois, I knew you know what it was. I got Lois Domain, what he said then, you know. Well after he sat in the band and taught me, because he used to coach me and tell me a lot of things, he can mention, valuable ideas about the trumpet, little tricks about the trumpet, you know. So after he sat in the band, before he went and played with us that night, he told me, he said, Anderson, I'm telling you what I'm doing, he said, man I'm going to take you and make you the first class trumpet player out of you, you've got to die, you know. He said, I'm going to bring them parts, I'm going to get those parts, make you get those parts down together. So that night when we started playing we had so much music to play, you know, because a young boy used to buy anything. So we had so much music to play that night, when he knocked off that night he said, I changed that. He said, I believe you'd better come over and instruct me. And Camilla Todd, the same way she's the piano player, she took Emily Hines to play, she took him with Aaron and I said, I'm surprised, because we used to play together, we had us in the Dixon Land band, you know. We had Willie Bontem, had Camilla Todd playing piano, had O.L. Foster, my cousin playing drums, I was playing trumpet, a fellow by the name of Gus Smatkart, he played trumpet. We had a nice little outfit, we played at the Columbia Crutch Club, you know. We made some time out there, I remember one night we made nine hours a piece, you know. Our side was fifteen hours, we left there with nine hours a piece, including our tips, you know. And one of those doctors tipped us so much he was kind of tipsy that night, you know, he just got a little bit too much in it. He wanted to play drums, nothing even wanted to play those drums, see. And the people in the place didn't want to play drums, you know. And every time he danced around he'd hand the drum about a ten dollar bill, see. He said, I guess that would make me play drums. So the drummer would let him play drums, see. And through that way we all got a plenty of tips. So what we knew him after that, we didn't like Doc, because Doc was a fine man, I said. So the next time Doc came in there, all of us hollering, hey Doc, how are you? He said, I think I said, all of you can go to hell. He said, I'm not drinking tonight. So don't be out of hand. So, after I left that bunch there, Handy took me off the Pelican. I said, I was playing on the Pelican, I was leading the band there, the Pelican band there, after the program left. Handy took me off the Pelican. He played the La Vida dance hall, the taxi dance. Alfred was playing drums there. He had Alfred playing drums, Handy the sax, Benny Turner playing piano, had I forget, one of the Hall brothers, you know, Clarence Hall, Edmund Hall, or the other brother, Robert Hall playing tenor. And we had, let's see, I think it was Manuel Sills playing guitar, yeah. He was playing banjo there, Manuel Sills, yeah. And I was playing trumpet. Well, I stayed there with them all about a year or so. So after, I tell you what, we went there one night to go to work, you know, and this guy, I forget his name, went to go to work and the place was locked on Monday night, which was pig night, see. So we went to the labor board to find us, and the man told us, I tell you one thing, these fellas fly by the night fellas, you all got to be careful playing for them. So some of them just in his business and said, soon as they make a good night, they're gone, you know. We never did get paid for that last week, I tell you. So what happened, we went to, the fella hired me at the Alamo dance hall. Well, Handy still kept his band. Handy had his Louisiana shaker, see. He had Alvin Alcorn with me, he went one way and I went on the Alamo, on the Canal Street, on Canal and Begun upstairs there, over at McCroys store there, it was Alamo there. Well I played there for quite a time, I think I must have played there about four years, around four years or something like that. And the man was running that place, took the Levita, Mr. Boyd took the Levita, see. Well I still work on the Levita for him, I went to the Levita for him after that. Played at the Levita. And from the Levita Gene Hall came in town and they hired me to play at the foreign dance hall, which is next door. Well at that time it was the Budweiser, the Budweiser people I had interest in, they had that great big eagle there, you know, on the outside. Well I was playing in that and old man they used to have some crowds and people in there. They had a bike in the back and a patio there. Place packed and jammed every night, you know, people made something out of that. And little young Danny got in a fight there with some soldier or something and hit the soldier.

He kind of hoity so, but he broke his own. And well the people know the Budweiser back and at least they want to sue the Budweiser people. So they backed out. See they had to go back to the front and they pulled out the interciser out of there. And after they played there about a few years, I can show you some words that a fella, we call him Mestedi. I don't know if you know him, he loved dances. A fella, he even reminded me of Mestedi. He used to come and that man would stand inside the band stand and he'd clap all night, so happy. He said, God, you boys, I swear to God, I don't know, that music just does something to me. He went home and I got to the world somewhere and he wrote just what he thought about the band and everything, it was a whole two or three pages, you know. What he thought about the music, you know. And I saw him about a couple of months ago on St. Charles Street, yes, and I played at the band. But why I said that too, I mean, yeah, it was foreign, it turned to be foreign. Well I played there when I, this Bill O'Connor came and got me from there to go to Entertainer's Cabaret, that's on, you know where that was, on the 25th. Franklin Street. Franklin Street, yeah, well that was in the National Army, entertain him. Well I went in there with Bill O'Connor and his riffers. Well that was the first time we broadcast, I was broadcasting with W.H.L. on Mondays. We used to go over there, and the same W.H.L. Williams was out singing with us, you know, everybody used to sing, you know. Well W.H.L. Williams was our vocalist. Understand? And he, first number, the only number, the first number he sang was Moonglow, it must have been Moonglow, you know. And I used to love the way he sang that, yeah. I played that to the entertainer's clothes, in other words, understand? Just about a week or two before they closed, Papa Celestan come for me, sent for me, see, because Heumann had left him to go with Joe Oliver. So Papa Celestan sent him. Herman, which Herman? Herman Franklin. He died, the late Heumann, yeah. Yeah. He died.
The guy used to be with Jimmy Gunn.
Yeah, he lived down in North Roche Blade Street, 1911.
He wrote a nice tune, that tune I'll have him home, and everybody said it, but I never heard

it. He said, like, so, Papa Celestan sent for me. Well, when Papa Celestan, see, I'll consider anybody in your arms, consider when you got a break with Papa Celestan, that was the best band in town, you know. He's going places, see, and I took the offer, and we really, they had a nice fine band. I stayed in that band. I went in that band in 1934, and stayed in Papa's band till 40, 41. Not a lot.
Yeah.

And then, 41, I went back to work a few weeks, a few months or so, at the foreign dance hall, the same dance hall, see. Well, then Uncle Sam called me there, and I had to go in army. Well, after Uncle Sam called me in army, I went in army. I took my trumpet with me when I got in army. A lot of fellas told me, I need to take that trumpet away. He said, man, we can have some fun. So I took the trumpet. And all on the train I was playing the trumpet, you know. And after I played the trumpet with the lieutenant, the fellas gave me a lot of privilege that I didn't usually get, you know. Let me get off the train. Once the soldiers get off, I'm going to get off the train and talk to people, you know. And when I went there, and I got in army at the reception center, I used to take my trumpet. Well, those numbers were very popular then. This heart of mine, this love of mine, this love of mine, you made me love, you know. Well, I got around the area and started blowing the trumpet, you see. Well, the lieutenants and the fellas around there got busy, they didn't want me to leave the camp, see. They didn't want me to stay there. It was impossible, see, when the soldiers got there, they got to carry you out, they got the trumpet, you know. But they did keep me there. All those fellas I came there with, I used to stand up there and blow up my butt and all that, you know, and say those blues things, they actually go for the lead.
Did you play in any army band or dances band there too?

Yes sir. So I'm coming to that now. So I left, I mean after these fellas, they took me and put me on KP one day, see, in the army, well every now and then I used to blow a tune, see, well they put me on KP. And the major, and then we missed the trumpet, he said, why is that fella playing that trumpet around there? I said, the fella from here, Sergeant Crude, he said, Italian fella. Oh he's on KP. He said, go get that, take that, go get that man. Let that man play that trumpet. So he came and brought another soldier, he said, soldier, grab that mock deck, come on now, chance. And he put me in the place, you know, where they send these boys, see these fellas that don't know how to dress, you know, their clothing. They send them back home, put them in the way to work, they send them clothes back home. He said, look, you stay in here and I don't care who comes for you, you stay in here and every now and then it blew me a little tune. So I stayed there in that little place, that little office, you know, and wait there until I left. But what was happening, they had several trumpet players come through, you know, and I put my trumpet on the mic, they'd call up their wives and their girlfriends, you know. And I put that mute in and play solos for them over there, you know. And the man said, oh, my wife said, that's great, you know. So they'd just do it for kicks, you know. Another trumpet said, come here, come here. I told the wife to them. I said, listen at this. She'd listen, they'd listen. See, they say, they ain't the same trumpet. I said, that's not the same trumpet they've been listening to. She said, you see that? All of them knew the difference. They don't even have to see, you see. So when I went, I got number one up there, we, we, in, in Eglinfield, Eglinfield, Florida. When I got there, they didn't have no band there. They had a white band, the 100 Air Force band. But we just got together, me and this fellow played with Bernie Johnson, Wallace Wilson, he's from Chicago. He and I got together and rounded up all the musicians, we got there and got us a little band, seven pieces. And we made out to play those marches for our company, you know, for the military music. And one day Arnold, General Arnold, you know, was coming to the field and Colonel Brent was over there then. Colonel Brent, I was passing through there, you know, me and three of the fellows passing over there, and he was back at the office, and he saw me at the Trump and said, come here, soldier. I'll come there where you know, because they got snapped attention when they talk. You know, we all snapped attention and still even, and I said, all right, as you were. He said, I'll call you in here and he said, I got a song here, saying I want you to play it. He said, I want you to take it back there and fix it up for the boys you bought, saying I want you all to play it tomorrow morning. He said, General Arnold is coming on the field, saying whatever you all do this song, you help me. So he said, run over it for me. So I took the trumpet and run over it. It was the engineer's fight song. He said, you know, you're the first man playing that song. I said, just come out of the press. He said, you're the first man playing the engineer's fight song. He said, and if you can play it like that, the band better play it tomorrow. I said, go back there and fix it up. And me and Wallace got together and wrote everybody part out, you know, half the next morning. We came with that, made us big shots with the conns, I mean with the general. Next morning we had a pleasure shaking hands with the general Arnold. So we played his song, you know, oh, when we played his song, Colonel Brent, you know, took his chest out, you know, and he walked up and shook out and saying, well when I get back I'm going to remember you all, you know. And it wasn't two weeks before he'd organized the 727 AAF band. You get lardy, you know, and that's when we band. Well after we got our band there, they sent the white band over. See, it was a kind of rule that a band had to be organized at least a year before you sent them out of the country. So that's what kept us on the side, see. Well, I got in the hospital sick, I mean, operated on my legs, cartilage, after leaving, I stayed in the hospital around sitting some days, you know. And I came out, when I came out the band, they tell me that the band won off, and some of them fellas, they said, the police didn't want enough soldiers to have a big band out there. Well it's wondering how many soldiers allowed, you know, they asked for it, and they gave it to them, you know. Well it's called a band. You understand? And when they did that, they had four of us. Because I told them, I said, well I told them, I said, if you all didn't want the band, I said, I'm going to play my trumpet. And I said, I'm going to get up in the morning and blow it. I used to get up and blow all I played. I used to get up and blow the bugle, all the boys to get up, you know. And I used to play this song about, da don't get around much anymore, you know. And I'd play that for the soldiers, and every time I'd hit that note they'd say, man you ain't a kid. Then I'd play sunny side of the street for them, you know, before I come back in. Well that would put them in a good mood, you know. And after that, they'd round all those busses boys, they'd send them on the field, they'd send one boy from the Algea, he's a male kid. They'd send them out and grab somebody in the mud. Because one of those musicians told me, he'd say, if you see Andy, tell him, he told me he's going to be playing his home when I come back. So they sent me in special service. I went to Virginia out there, to turn the peninsula. We had an organized little band out there, it had about six pieces. We called it the Dixieland band, you know. So we had, they say our band is better than Fort, out there in Cal, North Cal, I forget the name, but they had a band, Big Van, you know. But after we got it, those people were crazy about the band. And those lieutenants, the people enjoyed all kinds of music, you know. And the fellas used to ask me, even the colored fellas, they'd say, Andy, how y'all can do that? I'd say, we can't do that. I'd say, one man know a tune, you pick it up and start playing, everybody jump in and play it. I'd say, we don't play like that. See if everybody don't know the music, I'd say, we can't play. He'd say, but you fellas can just, just one man in the band, no tuning, hit it, and when he finished it, right in there on, it sounded like he was playing for you. I'd say, man, it's just, it's you on. So that's the way we do down in you on. So after that, the boys, I'm going to tell you about, after our band had broke up, you know, I went on the fine line, you know, we go on the fine line where you shoot, you know, like target practice, you know. And some gold brick went in there hanging around and set the tenor fire. And those people here gave me a beautiful overcoat, you know, you don't get them, you might look like different than anybody, you know. I burned my old coat up and my sister had sent me a cake and some candy, I burned all the candy up, it burned my trumpet up. I had a brand new king I went in there with. And that trumpet was perfect, it looked like I could make anything of it. It burned my trumpet up and I was worried about the trumpet, so I was shooting on the fine line and the lieutenant, the captain Jackson was giving his orders, you know, and all in the same breath, he said, and Andy Anderson, you look like you're worried since you're on the trumpet, you keep making all them bullseyes. He said, you look like you ought to be nervous. So when I come in the pay line, and the pay line, when I come through the pay line, I didn't know they were going to do this, you know. When I came through the pay line, I was playing payday the other night, they had a single box there. And when I came through the lute, all the lieutenants gave five dollars a piece, some of them ten dollars, you know. When I came there they had a hundred and forty dollars in there for me to go buy me a trumpet. So after I came there, I told the lute, I said, well I got to go buy me a trumpet. He said, I'll take you down and buy one. He took me down and buy a trumpet. When he got on the head of the money, he said, put your money in your pocket. I said, I'm paying for it. He'll take you a fuller with that money. So if he gave me that money, he bought me a trumpet. He said, he got one of the special service going, handed you everyone, and he said, but I'm going to buy this one for you. So he bought me a trumpet. And he bought me that trumpet and he wrote me a long letter, you know. And I had pictures of, you know, the band of the Papazelestand's band, you know, just little things happening, you know, the publicity stuff. And this long letter that they wrote for me, telling me how much they appreciated my playing, you know, in the Moira building, you know. And I know when I came out on the furlough, some of the fellas were jealous, you know. See we'd move out of there. Some of them took the pictures and everything and threw them and it rained on me. Everything just tore up at me. And even letters, see I wouldn't take a million dollars for that letter of recommendation, man. That was the thing, you know. I regret it. As far as the pictures were concerned, I forget some more pictures sometimes. But that letter was signed by the lieutenants there, you know, well how they appreciate my playing and everything.
I keep interrupting you, but I forgot to ask you something more. When you were growing up, who were some of your favorite trumpet players?

Well my favorite trumpet players was one, I'll tell you, one fella I admired for the style of playing. Pete Lacarre was one, see. I also admired Kid Punch. That's another one. Kid Punch and Pete Lacarre. I'll tell you another fella too, I admired playing too, was Kid Rainey. Kid Rainey I admired his playing too.
Did you say you heard Bunk over there?

Oh Bunk, Bunk and so on. I got my inspiration to pick up the trunk through Bunk's playing, see. Because I was a little kid when Bunk used to my home. We didn't wear no pants, they had those little long shapes on, you know. The boys, you know. And we used to go to the, see, go to the dance, you know. And he used to kid us, the way we used to ask my daddy for pop, you know, so cool. So I used to say, pop, give me a bottle of pop.
Oh did you remember Tommy Ladner over there?

Yes, he's from my home. Yeah, he's a, daddy had a place out there on the highway, you know. And he was like, yeah he was a blues player, you know. I wasn't thinking about playing trumpet, but I had it in my mind, it was a dream then, you know. And I had it in my mind, but after the tournament, I'm surprised he ever thought that Tommy had got great. He was one of the greatest blues trumpet players ever in Chicago. I heard that. And Bunk used to come over to my home, see, on those weekends, sometimes he'd stay all the way, but Bunk was a mischievous guy, you know. I mean it was no harmony, but it was just mischievous like that, when he'd get to drinking in the booze, he would, oh he's bad on drums, see, he'd always ride the drummer. Little Clay Bear, you know, Cagman that is brother? Used to play drums somewhere over there. And my daddy had that little three piece playing, you see, and when they come off, see, they played at the parks, at Jackson Park over the lake there, from eight to twelve, winning knockoff. Those colored dances went all night, see, they played the summer. From twelve to twelve, see, the sun would be shining, because I was a kid, I'd go to sleep, and when I'd wake up and look out the window, the sun would be riding, I'd hear the music still playing, see, over there. Over there.

In other words they'd play until they sold everything, the gum, the ham, the chicken, everything out. That's what the band played. The price of admission wasn't much then, a thirty cents or a forty cents or something like that. Yeah, Bunk was a great guy. I think he was a great, I'll tell you what Bunk's playing, I like about Bunk's playing in 5th. I mean it looked like he put all his whole heart, soul and mind on every note he made. Looked like he talked to them and so on. And it was great. He was great. And then he could blow loud too, it's another thing. He could blow soft too. We had a, he had a sister live over there, you know, her name was Bertha Jackson. Her and her husband, they lived about, oh my, let's say 50 or 60 feet from where we were living in our homes. And his sister and her husband, his name was Vara, used to fight every Saturday night. He'd get hired and come in there and tip, all his furniture, tip everything. And then Monday morning he'd go down and buy some more dishes and stuff. And Bunk was just as mysterious as he could be, you know. He'd get some foolish booze and come around and he'd meet people just for fun, you know. He wasn't a bad fellow. Oh no.
What about that fight between Big Cornish and Dad? You tell me about that once. Oh I'll tell you about Cornish and Dad.

And I'll tell you about Conius II. Conius II was another guy who had a fight. I didn't laugh at him, that you know, and he was playing gettoes them day. You see, gettoes started out in Dixieland, you know. And then the banjo took off, but getto was the first, you know. But he got the banjo because getto was in there to improvise then. The gipho was too soft, you know. That's when the banjo would come in. Well Cornish and Dad was a little bit of a fellow, you know. Oh, Cornish is about seven feet, you know. And Dad was a little old fellow about three feet high, probably three feet I guess. So when they'd get tight, you know, both of them would always like to fight with one another, you know. But Cornish would be playing with him, you know, and Dad would be hit, Cornish would hit at Dad, you know, and Dad would run between Cornish's legs. Dad would run between Cornish's legs.
Okay, it's going again.

Yeah, and I finished talking about little Dad. Yeah, I finished that too. I finished talking about little Dad and Cornish. So, Cornish used to kid Dad, you know, all the time. Well Dad's a little bit of a fellow, you know, he'd say, I'm a man boy. He'd say, but I'm a small man. But I got plenty of brains out of him. I got plenty of brains out of him. And he'd go and he'd start, oh, you know, he wasn't fighting, but Cornish would be playing with him, you know. But he'd be juicing, he thought, you know. He'd start hitting that Cornish and Cornish would hit at him like that, you know, and he'd run through, Dad would run through Cornish's leg. And Octave told me that Dad went out to, when he took Dad to Mexico, you know, little Dad, Octave told me, Crosby told me, I said, took Dad to Mexico, saying, you know, Octave doesn't drink, you know, he ain't drink anything, saying, Dad went out and got full of the Mexican, you know, Chiquilla, you know what it was called. He said, Dad come down the road hooping. Whoop! He said, I done killed 40 Mexicans and I killed them. He said, I think, grand, he said, come here boy. He said, those people can throw a knife and block you. So, yeah, so I mean, I ended up, I happened to play with another band I went with, I'll tell you, the band I went with was P-Run, AJ P-Run's band. I played with them, I made a trip with them on the boat, on the steam jazz, but we had to get off there in St. Louis and play on the President also, you know, because there were two bands and, well, I went up there with them, we had a trip up there, the band was consisted of myself, Joe Phillips, Eddie Pearson playing Tramon, P-Jone, well P-Jone led the band, he did all the, mostly the band, the first band, P-Jone did most of the leading, and Manuel Sells, the late Boecker, Washington, and let's see who else named, Arthur Durabney, and what was the brother, Ruzon I think it was playing, Ruzon, and John Kazma's brother, Bill, playing tenor. Let's see, I believe that's all, yeah, we had Louis Barber and playing drums, Louis Barber and playing drums, that band, he had a fine band at that time. I took Leo Dajon to play at that time, you know, and went up for us, so Joe Phillips said, when I went up there, because Leo Dajon plays a much different mind, you know, my style was different from him, you know, but when I first went on the boat, the captain didn't like my playing, you know, like, because Leo had such a, and it's true a fella, you know, if you're used to listening to that trumpet, it'd be different, you know, so after I went on the boat and stayed up there, we got there, so Joe Phillips said, man, he said, if you're going to get to Memphis, Tennessee, if you have your trumpet there and your uniform, say you done got cap, you know. I said, yeah, so when we got to Memphis, Tennessee, the uniforms and the trumpet and everything was there for me, you know. I know after I left there, somewhere around, I didn't like the boat, you know, for some reason, after I hadn't gone that far, you know, all the fellas liked it, but I mean, it was kind of rough, you know, you play all evening and then you got to play at night too, you know, you play those picnics or those. Sometimes a day, clock in the morning, picnics all day, you know, and you play in the evening. So when we got to them, where I got to, I told Peter that I want to leave, you know, so they asked me to stay two more weeks. If I stay two more weeks, he'll give them my fare back. So I decided to stay two more weeks, two more weeks. Well, after that, he couldn't get nobody to come, you know. So he sent for Pajou, I believe. But Pajou hadn't come, though, when I left. Joe Phillips had to play for his trumpet. So Joe Phillips had to play for his trumpet, see. So, we went down to, people went down to talk to him, brought me down to talk to him, and he's asking me to stay, you know. So he said, well, you got to forget about what I said and what I thought. I told him, I said, well, it wasn't that a fella, but I said, well, I got an interest in the band, because we had a band, Celestine Band, it was a band, you know, it was a company band, you know. And you had stock, like you bought all those automobiles, you know, and all the things, well, you lose that, you know, if you stay away from the band, you know. So I tell him, I said, no, I have interest in the band, I'm playing with Tuxi, the band, I said, I've been playing with them, and I decided to go back, go back with the band, you know. He said, well, no, he said, you look like you're angry, because I said, well, I said, let me tell you one thing. He said, I fired Lil Armstrong on this boo. He said, look where he's at. I said, well, I fired Lil Armstrong, he said, and about me saying anything about you. He said, I found out after you got up here, he said, now when you go down the ass, I didn't know. He said, but I found out after you got up, since you had, you been up here around these people, saying, those people are crazy about the band, so you got, in that time, I had a band, you know, say, you got a Benny Goodman band, one of the greatest swing bands, you know, ever come up the rim. So then Fat Fischer got angry with him, he and Fat, I mean, he and Fess had some words about it, so Fess got asked me to interfere in the band, so Fess thought I was angry too about it, but I wasn't, you know. Really, I came on back home, I just want to come back, you know. So I left the boat in Denport, Iowa, and went to Chicago and stayed there. My uncle offered me a place to stay free a month. I should have stayed, I don't know, but he loved New Orleans, but the South I came over here, he said, I'm going to give you a place to stay and feed you a month, and if you don't get a break in that time, you can go back home. I don't know, just love, New Orleans. I came on back home, see, and never did go back anymore. And I played on this. This boat go across, these guys, I was taking a camellia. I used to play on that plencher boat running across Lake Pontius Rang, you know. I played on that regla, me and Ruben Hughes, and Ruben McClennis, Lil Bob, he's dead, like Bob Davis, Jim Davis' brother, you know, playing drum and let's see who else would play piano. Sadie was playing piano. Yeah, Sadie was playing piano. I played on that. That was a nice job. I used to enjoy that, because you used to enjoy the nice ride, you know, hitting the cool, peep a nice peep. What about Cornelius? You were going to tell me about him. Oh yeah, Cornelius, yeah. Cornelius, you know when they used to tie those trucks up, you know when the band thought they were better than the other band, they wouldn't pull off, you know. But some guy would get there with the ropes, and he said, no you can't pull off, we're going to tie them all together. And Cornelius, and the bass player, I forget the bass player, the other big was wallpaper. I think it was wallpaper. But I only got the organ, you know. And Cornelius took his guitar and hit the back of it like that, and when he hit the wallpaper, his head went through the guitar, see. Well, naturally the guitar broke, and his head got caught in there, you know. And the funniest thing is he could hear you're pulling through. And those guys laughed out a week, laughed a week about that. It didn't hurt him, man, though. Yeah, it didn't hurt him. I mean, how funny it was, you know. He hit it with the guitar, and it went down his head, you know. And then they locked his head in there, you know. When they had he couldn't see the man, he was pulling, you know. Shoved him off from there and pulled him like that, you know. And those guys, man, had some fun. Buddy Petit, get it in there.
I've been asked about him playing across the lake, too. Did you ever do that?

Oh yeah, he was a nice, he was a nice drummer. I'll tell you about Buddy Petit, what I love about Buddy Petit. He couldn't make no high notes like Lou Armstrong, but he did make everything that Lou Armstrong made, see. That's one thing about this song, you know. I love that, you know. And he could play you a beautiful second by head, you know, just by air like that. Makes some pretty parts. I do some of them now, you know. Some of them try to do something, remind me of him, you know. Some of those things you hear about from you. Yeah, when the band be playing, I try to pick up some of those little harmony parts. You know, he used to play in that, the second part. The thing I used to like to hear him play was Baby Face, you know. He's talking about putting a pretty part in there. The clarinet would take the lead, the trombone, you know. And he'd put that little second part in there. He's talking about sounding pretty. Did you hum a little bit? That's the way he would play it? You know the part so? Something like that. I can't get it. Yeah, I know what you mean though. The second part down. But it was a pretty part. You know, with the little tones he made, they were so pretty, you know. It was touching. It was touching, that's right. It was touching, the blue part he made. And he used to have a beautiful tone in the trombone, you know. I used to admire his playing. He was another long song, but he just didn't have the amateur, you know. He played the higher notes.
He played all the other little fast things.
Yeah, and he was a genius on the diminished chords, you know. He could make up some diminished chords, it was great, you know. You make them pretty too.
Do you remember Bunk style enough? Was Buddy Petit anything like Bunk style?

No, I don't think. I don't think it all was. I just think it was a musician, a rhythm musician, trying to make a chance. No. I think Bunk had a rhythm style of his own. You take Buddy Petit, he had his style, you know. Buddy Petit had a style similar to Lil Armstrong, see. Only he couldn't play all those high notes, you know. Kid Rainey was a nice, keen tone trumpet. He played high, you know. He played like that all the time. He used to practice things with the melody below and he played above the stage, you know. That's another guy who played a nice, sweet trumpet. And those two would do two different, Bunk was different, see. But I think Buddy Petit had Lil Armstrong style of the chord. Now Kid Punch, he was a different trumpet player. He played a kind of what we call a chord style, but it would be a major chord. He'd go, dun you know, like that. Dun like that. And he'd play all the way through like that. And he had some beautiful runs he'd make, you know. The breaks, he was great at that. Kid Punch was great at that. But not the Minish, things like that. They did. The kid, he played too, but Buddy Petit was the king of the Minish. Yeah. He played a lot of those. Made him pretty too, you know. The band would make a breaking lay out there, man. And he'd come in there and hit one of the Minish cards, man. Knock you out. I tried to make some of them, you know. Playing feel good. But I don't practice them like that, you know. But they are pretty. I remember when I was playing with the Papa Celestan band, we got a fan that are from somewhere around New York. They used to listen out of a band. And I remember what they said, and they were telling the truth. They said the band had a great band to tell the saxophones to practice more diminished chords, you know, and use them where they're. And they were telling the truth, because the boys were there. Alaba Alcorn, he used to play them sometimes. But Clarence Hall would very seldom, he'd play them in the Divinity. But Alaba Alcorn, he used to play them. But that's the chord. That's the chord I like to see when it falls, you know. When it falls in there and make a diminished chord. I tell you who makes a lot of it too now. He makes them pretty much Thomas Jefferson. Yeah.
Well, as I change the subject while I think of it, across the lake I'm wondering about the music there, since most people over here don't know it. Do you remember Isidore Fritz?

Isidore Fritz was one of the greatest clarinetists we had. Jazz kinder. He was nothing but a jazz kinder. He didn't read no music. And he could play anything you play and put harmony to anything you know.
I know George Lewis talks about him being wonderful. I wonder if anybody else ever heard him.
George Lewis got his style from him. George Lewis was coming along.
He really was great you think too?
He was a great player. All the musicians think so, because most everyone went over there and played them there.
He never came over on this side of the lake though I guess.
He never would. He was a brick mace you know.
What kind of a band did he play in do you remember?
They had the Independent Band. That's the band that Bunk played with them.
Oh Bunk played with that band.
Yeah that band. That's the band. They had a fine band. They had Isidore Fritz, Louis Fritz, his brother playing trombone, his daddy playing bass, old man Joe Fritz.
He had a bunk playing trumpet and this boy Leon Loron was playing guitar with him.
What's his name?

Leon Loron. He's still old guitar player there with him. And then Ralph used to play violin with my dad. His brother Ralph Loron used to play violin with my daddy. He was a great violinist too. Baye, you know. He played both the same thing. And the drummer, the drummer I tell you was playing with him was clay bad. Little clay bad. His name is Keglin Eddie's brother. He's dead now. He's late clay bad. Well that was they lined up. And they had a fine band. Normally they play all those old moments such as the Tiger, Rag.
Did they work over there very often?

Oh yeah they worked on Friday, Saturday and Sunday. When Buddy Petit came over to work, he usually worked about a week. He played the vicinity like he'd take us out there. After Buddy Petit, he worked for this fellow LeBlanc. Mr. LeBlanc, he's up there on, incidentally I saw him a few weeks ago, he's up there on Maple Street. So LeBlanc took them over there and had a station wagon, see. Now he booked dances every night, you know. He'd play one, on Monday night he'd play in Mandeville. On Saturday night, Tuesday night, no he'd play in Carpentry. On Wednesday night he'd go to Bougalusa, you understand? Well Thursday night he'd play in Picayune or something like that, see. And then he'd come back to Mandeville and they'd play Friday, Saturday and Sunday at Votran's place on the beach, you know on the lake there? Mandeville on the beach. But those other nights, he kept them busy, you know, because I used to go around with them and be the doorman for them, you know. They had a real good band, they had a really good jazz band.

Any other questions? Dick, do we want to finish up with Mandeville? No, I don't think I think we better get on out. All right, unless you have something you want to add about your life to fill out something in a minute?

Oh, my life, I tell you all, my life is up now, just the way I feel about music now, you know. I play music so long when I'm getting too old to do anything else. And anywhere where I can play my horn and make a living, it's not too full for me to go. You understand? I'll go any place so I can be happy playing my horn and making a living.
You've played a lot of brass band work.

You've played brass band, I played Tuxi the brass band with John, made the recording with John, made the recording with John, a couple of LPs we cut with John, brass band, cut some LPs with George Lewis' band. Also went to play the festival last year with all the big shots, Coleman Hawkins. Los Angeles. Yeah, we were in Monterey, California. Oh, up there. Yeah, that's right. Yes, sir. What's your call, my mom? Woody Hoyman, Hawkins, Roy Irish, Oil Hines, Sarah Vones.
Yeah, I remember we read about that. What's the lady's name, Homer?

The lady's singing? I can't remember thinking of her name. From here? Yeah, the jazz singer. Lizzie Miles. Lizzie Miles, she was on the program too. Chris Barberin, he was there too. He was there on the, yeah.
Oh yeah, well. All those guys. We hope you have a lot of success and you're still a young man and go a long way.
I hope so and thanks for everything, yeah.
Okay, we're going to finish up with Alfred on the same reel.

segments.title: Opening, name, birthplace Mandeville and birth date
segments.summary: Tape identification, full name Andrew Joe Anderson, born in Mandeville across the lake, 10 August 1905; Bunk played there with his father.

segments.title: Learning trumpet, Willie Foster's band and the Pelican band
segments.summary: His father's spasm band, buying a cornet, correspondence course and lessons, joining Willie Foster, then the Pelican band with its coaching, new arrangements and raided personnel.

segments.title: Clarence Todd and Camilla Todd, pianists in the Pelican band
segments.summary: Clarence Todd, his sister Camilla and Clarence Williams recordings come up in discussion.

segments.title: Dixieland band at the club, then Handy's dance-hall jobs and the Alamo
segments.summary: Coaching from Leo Dejan, the Dixieland band's big tips night, then Handy's La Vida band, the Alamo and the foreign dance hall.

segments.title: Bill O'Connor broadcasts and joining Papa Celestin's band
segments.summary: A fan's letter, broadcasting with Bill O'Connor's band, then Celestin sends for him; he stays in Celestin's band from 1934 to 1940-41.

segments.title: Called up in 1941 and taking his trumpet to the reception center
segments.summary: Back at the dance hall, drafted, and playing trumpet on the train and at the reception center.

segments.title: Army band at Eglin Field, special service and the replacement trumpet
segments.summary: Forming a band at Eglin Field, the engineer's fight song, special service in Virginia and the lieutenants buying him a trumpet.

segments.title: Favorite trumpet players growing up
segments.summary: He names Pete Lacarre, Kid Punch and Kid Rainey as trumpeters he admired.

segments.title: Bunk Johnson and Tommy Ladnier playing across the lake
segments.summary: Bunk's visits to his father's place in Mandeville, Tommy Ladnier, the all-night dances at the park, and Bunk's playing and mischief.

segments.title: Big Cornish and little Dad fight stories
segments.summary: Banjo and guitar remarks, and the comic fights between tall Cornish and tiny Dad, who ran between his legs.

segments.title: Dad in Mexico, Piron riverboat trip, lake boat job and Cornelius's guitar
segments.summary: More on Dad, then his trip on the steamer with Piron's band, leaving the boat, the Pontchartrain boat job, and Cornelius's head through a guitar.

segments.title: Buddy Petit's playing and style compared with Bunk, Kid Rainey and Kid Punch
segments.summary: Buddy Petit's pretty second parts and diminished chords, how his style differed from Bunk's, and other trumpeters' styles.

segments.title: Isidore Fritz, the great clarinetist who stayed across the lake
segments.summary: Fritz as a self-taught jazz clarinetist who influenced George Lewis and never crossed the lake.

segments.title: The Independent Band and LeBlanc's dance bookings across the lake
segments.summary: Lineup of the Independent Band with Bunk, the Frits and Lorons, and LeBlanc's nightly dance circuit around Mandeville.

segments.title: His attitude to music and life now
segments.summary: He says he will go anywhere to play his horn and make a living.

segments.title: Brass band LPs, George Lewis recordings and the Monterey festival
segments.summary: Brass band work, LPs with George Lewis's band and the festival at Monterey with Hawkins, Hines, Lizzie Miles and others.
